title: Seed Germination Lab
subtitle: Wake the seed — and discover what a plant needs to begin.

learningFocus.summary: In this lab the student works as an investigator, running a fair test to discover what a dormant seed needs before it will germinate. They practise the core skills of scientific enquiry — making a prediction, changing one variable at a time while holding the others constant, and reading quantitative results straight from their own trials. Interpreting the germination data builds analytical and mathematical reasoning as they link temperature, oxygen and light to a measurable percentage outcome, and explaining why sealing off the air stops growth develops the critical-thinking habit of reasoning from evidence to mechanism — that the embryo needs oxygen for respiration to release the energy for growth. Applying the pattern to a real gardening problem strengthens problem-solving and written communication using precise scientific vocabulary: seed coat, embryo, cotyledon, germination. The content practised is USDP Junior High Life Science 6 (Term 1, Module 5: Green Plant) — the structure of a seed and the conditions required for germination — laying the groundwork for later study of photosynthesis and plant life cycles.

orient.objective: Discover the conditions a seed needs to germinate — warmth, water and oxygen — and explain why, using the parts of the seed.
orient.courseLink: Life Science 6, Term 1, Module 5: Green Plant. This is the groundwork for photosynthesis and plant life cycles later in the course.
successCriteria: Name the four parts of a seed and say what each one does.
Run a fair test — change one condition at a time — to find what a seed needs to germinate.
Explain why a seed with no oxygen will not grow, using the word respiration.
orient.mission: A seed is a tiny plant, packed and waiting. Your job as lab scientist is to find out what makes a sleeping seed wake up and start to grow — and why different seeds want different things.
steps: Meet the seed. Open the seed diagram and learn its four parts: seed coat, embryo, cotyledon and first leaf.
Predict what a seed needs before you test anything.
Run trials in the Germination Chamber. Change the temperature, the oxygen and the light, and watch what happens.
Your results save into your Investigation Record by themselves.
Explain the pattern, apply it to real gardening, then answer the Knowledge Check.
Press Generate Learning Evidence to download your work to hand in.
orient.realLife: You have seen this on your own kitchen counter. Cress or beans sprout on damp cotton in a few warm days, but seeds left in a cold, sealed, or bone-dry place just sit there. Farmers and gardeners choose exactly when and how deep to sow every seed for the same reasons you are about to discover.

predict.prompt: Before you touch the chamber: which THREE things do you think every seed must have to start germinating?
predict.hint: Pick the three you believe are essential. You will get to change your mind after your trials.

investigate.title: The Germination Chamber
investigate.lede: Choose a seed, set the conditions, and press Incubate. Water is always provided and kept the same — that way any change you see is caused by the factor you changed.

record.intro: Every trial you incubate is logged here automatically. This is your evidence — no copying by hand.
record.emptyText: No trials yet. Go back to the Germination Chamber and incubate a seed.

explain.prompt: Look back at your Investigation Record. Explain what happened to germination when you lowered the oxygen right down, and say WHY that happened.
explain.lede: Use the numbers from your own trials as evidence.
explain.frame: Try this shape: "When I lowered the oxygen to ___%, germination dropped to ___%. This happened because a seed needs oxygen for ___, which releases the ___ it needs to grow."
explain.placeholder: When I lowered the oxygen to…
expectedPoints: Quotes their own low-oxygen trial result (e.g. germination near 0% when oxygen was ~1-3%).
States that a seed / embryo needs oxygen for respiration.
Explains respiration releases the energy the embryo needs to grow, so with little or no oxygen there is not enough energy and the seed cannot germinate.

apply.prompt: A gardener sows lettuce seeds in the middle of a hot summer. They bury the seeds deep in the soil and the weather sits at about 35°C. Hardly any lettuce comes up. Use what you discovered to give TWO reasons why.
apply.lede: This is a real problem gardeners face. Think about what lettuce seed needs.
apply.frame: Give two clear reasons. Think about temperature and light, and remember what is (and is not) deep underground.
expectedPoints: Lettuce seed needs light to germinate; buried deep it is in darkness, so few germinate.
Lettuce is a cool-season seed; 35°C is above its temperature range, so heat stops it germinating (dormancy).
Reasoning links a named factor (light and/or temperature) to the failure, not just 'it was too hot' with no mechanism. Bonus: deep soil also holds less oxygen.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Match each part of the seed to its job.

pairs.right: A tough outer layer that protects the seed
The tiny baby plant that will grow
A food store that feeds the young plant at first
The first true leaf that makes food using light

knowledgeCheck.explain: The seed coat guards the embryo. The embryo is the baby plant. Cotyledons are packed lunch. Once the first true leaf opens, the plant starts making its own food by photosynthesis.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: In your trials, seeds sealed with almost no oxygen did not germinate. Which life process needs oxygen to release the energy a seed uses to start growing?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Respiration uses oxygen to release energy from the seed's food store. No oxygen means no energy, so the seed cannot grow.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Lettuce seeds left in a dark drawer barely germinated, but the same seeds on a bright windowsill grew well. What does lettuce seed need that many other seeds do not?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Lettuce is light-sensitive: its seeds need a flash of light to break dormancy. Most seeds germinate fine in the dark, underground — but not lettuce.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A seed needs oxygen for respiration. Roughly what percentage of the air around us is oxygen?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Air is about 21% oxygen (and roughly 78% nitrogen). That is plenty for a seed — until you seal the air away.

rubric.note: You are graded out of 15 marks, shown as a percentage. The Knowledge Check is marked for you automatically; your teacher marks the two written answers.

criteria.label: Knowledge & understanding
criteria.descriptor: Seed parts, why oxygen matters, the light rule, and the oxygen level of air — all correct in the Knowledge Check.

criteria.label: Use of evidence
criteria.descriptor: Your Explain answer quotes real numbers from your own Investigation Record.

criteria.label: Scientific reasoning
criteria.descriptor: Your Apply answer reasons correctly about a new situation, linking temperature and light to germination.

criteria.label: Communication
criteria.descriptor: Clear, full sentences using the right words: seed coat, embryo, cotyledon, first leaf, germination.

aiMarkingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply) using the rubric and each question's expected_points. The Knowledge Check is already auto-marked in auto_marked_score — copy it into knowledge_accuracy (7 marks = full). For Explain, award use_of_evidence (max 3): full marks if the student quotes their own low-oxygen trial number AND correctly links it to respiration releasing energy. For Apply, award reasoning (max 3): full marks for two correct, mechanism-based reasons (light needed but buried in dark; temperature above lettuce's range). Award communication (max 2) across both answers for clear sentences and correct use of the terms seed coat, embryo, cotyledon, first leaf, germination. Accept scientifically valid alternative wording and do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Total is out of 15; report the percentage, one strength, one correction, and one next step, in under 80 words.
